description: Freefall Labs is a team building an interactive dashboard for NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments. We bring scattered results from ISS fire research into one place, where you can filter experiments, compare measurements on a single chart, and rank findings by relevance to Moon and Mars missions. AI summaries and answers always cite the papers they come from, and the ranking formula is visible and adjustable.
summary:
Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into clear answers about spacecraft and Moon-base fire safety. It loads BASS-II and 13 other investigations from NASA's PSI database and ranks them for crew-habitat relevance with transparent, adjustable criteria.

The centerpiece is our playable flame sandbox. Built on a custom WebAssembly engine, it lets you paint 25 materials onto a grid, place fans, and watch fire spread through temperature, oxygen, airflow, CO₂ and camera views. You can load any of 129 real NASA BASS-II tests, run them, and compare the simulated outcome with what NASA measured. A Moon-base what-if reruns a real test at 34% oxygen and lunar gravity, clearly marked as extrapolation.

Our key finding is that no solid-material test reaches Moon-base oxygen levels, and PSI holds no partial-gravity data yet. The dashboard never fills missing values, labels gaps as gaps, and ranks evidence, not danger. Built with Next.js, Payload CMS, Postgres, Recharts, Three.js and WebAssembly.
details:
Freefall's Flame is a web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into clear answers about fire safety for crewed spaceflight. It loads BASS-II and 13 other investigations from NASA's PSI database, ranks them for crew-habitat fire safety, and shows where the evidence stops.

What it does and how it works

  • Investigations: the 14 PSI investigations appear as cards, ranked on five criteria with adjustable weights. Rankings measure how much evidence exists, not how dangerous a material is.
  • Moon-base card: it sets 34% O₂ and 0.17 g against what the tables actually hold. No solid-material test goes above 22.2% O₂, and PSI has no partial-gravity data yet.
  • Evidence and Visualization: materials are scored by coverage, and a heatmap marks empty cells as gaps rather than proof of safety. Charts cover gas composition before and after tests, airflow against oxygen use, and a plot-any-two-columns tool. The raw table shows censored readings as recorded, never as zeros.
  • Interpretation: an AI chatbot (Claret) can list and explain investigations and open the sandbox. The model sees only the checked-in catalogue, not raw data, and answers that invent numbers are rejected. Without an AI key, a deterministic fallback runs instead.
  • Sandbox: a playable flame simulator on a custom WebAssembly engine. Users paint 25 materials, place fans, watch temperature, oxygen, flow, CO₂, CO and camera views, and load any of 129 NASA BASS-II test presets to compare the simulated outcome with NASA's. A Moon-base what-if reruns a real NASA test at 34% O₂ and lunar gravity, marked as extrapolation.
  • Conclusions, Sources, Customize: findings and recommendations, a page documenting every table, paper and assumption, and a theme picker with 20 palettes.
  • Your own data: admins add a dataset, define its columns and upload a CSV. It is validated and published to the same dashboard.

Benefits and intended impact
Researchers and engineers can see in minutes which experiments cover a habitat condition and where nothing exists. By showing that solid materials have not been tested at Moon-base oxygen, we want to point the next experiments, such as LUCI and FM2, at that gap. The same pipeline works for any dataset and carries over to fire safety on Earth.

Tools used
Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Payload 3 CMS on Postgres, S3-compatible storage, Tailwind CSS 4, Recharts, Three.js, PapaParse, the AI SDK with OpenRouter, a WebAssembly C engine for the sandbox, and Vitest and Playwright for tests. Data comes from NASA PSI and NTRS.

What's creative about it

  • The sandbox turns NASA data into something you can play with. Instead of only reading tables, users paint 25 materials onto a grid, place fans, and watch fire spread on a custom WebAssembly engine. They can load any of 129 real BASS-II tests, run them, and compare the simulated outcome with what NASA measured. A Moon-base what-if reruns a real test at 34% oxygen and lunar gravity, clearly marked as extrapolation.
  • The analysis is built around honesty. It ranks how much evidence exists, never how dangerous a material is. Missing values are never filled in, censored readings stay as recorded, and an empty heatmap cell means "untested", not "safe". Every number comes from deterministic, tested code, and AI only explains it, with its answers checked against the data and rejected if they invent figures. The ranking weights are adjustable, so users can see how the order changes.
  • The interface is a JupyterLab-style workspace. Tabs open in resizable panes that users can split, dock and rearrange, and the layout is remembered between visits. A researcher can put the sandbox beside the evidence heatmap, or a chart next to the NASA papers behind it, and work the way they would in a notebook.

What we considered

  • Scientific limits: microgravity is not lunar gravity, gas readings are not fire outcomes, and the sandbox ignores pressure.
  • Reproducibility: column mapping is deterministic, and ambiguous matches are flagged instead of guessed.
  • Safety and cost: the AI model is fixed, rate-limited, capped daily and cached.
  • Audience: researchers, students and engineers, from a quick overview to raw rows.
